faqs.q: How much does a Shiba Inu cost to buy?
faqs.a: Reputable breeders typically charge $500–$2,000 for a Shiba Inu puppy. Prices vary by breeder reputation, health testing, and lineage. Rescue adoption fees are typically $100–$500 and include vaccinations, neutering, and microchipping.

faqs.q: What is the monthly cost of owning a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Budget $120–$200 per month for a Shiba Inu, covering food, preventive vet care, insurance, grooming and supplies. Small breeds often cost less on food and some products, but vet bills don't proportionally reduce — procedures cost similar amounts regardless of size.

faqs.q: What are the biggest ongoing costs for a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: The three largest annual expenses are food ($300–600), veterinary care ($400–$1,200 budgeted annually), and pet insurance ($$400–$1,200 per year). Grooming costs are lower for short-coated breeds managed at home.

faqs.q: How much does a Shiba Inu cost in the first year?
faqs.a: Year one costs for a Shiba Inu are significantly higher than subsequent years, typically $1,500–$3,000. This covers the purchase price or adoption fee, initial vet checks, vaccinations, spay/neuter, microchipping, crate, bedding, collar, leads and puppy training classes.

faqs.q: How often should I groom a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus need brushing 3–5 times per week, daily during seasonal coat blows. The dense undercoat requires a dedicated undercoat rake, not just a surface slicker brush. Nails should be trimmed every 3–4 weeks. Ears should be checked and cleaned monthly.

faqs.q: Do Shiba Inus shed a lot?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus have seasonal shedding — manageable with a consistent brushing routine.

faqs.q: What grooming tools does a Shiba Inu need?
faqs.a: A slicker brush for surface debris and an undercoat rake for the dense undercoat are both essential. A shedding blade or deshedding tool helps during heavy moult periods. A nail grinder is useful if your Shiba Inu is sensitive to clippers.

faqs.q: How often should I bathe a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Every 4–6 weeks is appropriate for most Shiba Inus that live indoors. More frequent bathing is needed if they swim or spend time in mud. Over-bathing strips natural skin oils — use a pH-balanced dog shampoo rather than human products.

faqs.q: Are Shiba Inus easy to train?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus are independent thinkers and can be challenging to train. They respond best to high-value rewards and clear, consistent criteria. A structured puppy class from week one is strongly recommended.

faqs.q: What training method works best for a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Reward-based training using treats, praise and toy rewards is the most effective and well-researched approach for Shiba Inus. Clicker training with precise timing works well to mark the exact moment of correct behaviour. Avoid aversive methods — they increase anxiety and often create secondary behavioural problems.

faqs.q: At what age should I start training my Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Start training from the day your puppy arrives home, typically at 8 weeks. The 8–16 week window is the most sensitive socialisation period. Enrol in a puppy class within the first two weeks for structured socialisation alongside basic obedience foundations.

faqs.q: How long does it take to train a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can take longer to reach reliable obedience than easier-to-train breeds — expect 3–6 months of consistent daily training for solid basics. Their independent nature means results compound slowly but durably with patience.

faqs.q: What health problems do Shiba Inus commonly have?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus are most commonly associated with brachycephalic airway issues. Regular vet checks, appropriate weight management, and breed-specific screening tests help detect issues early. Ask any breeder for health test results before purchasing.

faqs.q: How long do Shiba Inus live?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus have an average lifespan of 13–16 years. Small breeds often live longer than large breeds. Dental care is particularly important for small dogs, as dental disease is a common longevity issue.

faqs.q: Are Shiba Inus prone to hip dysplasia?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus have a moderate-to-elevated risk of hip dysplasia, particularly for large or active breeds. Ask for OFA or PennHIP hip evaluation certificates when buying from a breeder. Weight control and avoiding high-impact exercise during bone growth (under 18 months) reduces risk.

faqs.q: What health tests should a Shiba Inu puppy have?
faqs.a: At minimum, your Shiba Inu puppy should have a vet health check, first vaccinations, deworming, and microchipping before coming home. Ask the breeder for parent health certificates relevant to Shiba Inu-specific conditions. A vet check within 72 hours of bringing your puppy home is recommended to establish a baseline.

faqs.q: Are Shiba Inus good with kids?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can be protective and may be cautious around unfamiliar children. Early socialisation with children from puppyhood significantly improves tolerance. Always supervise interactions between dogs and young children.

faqs.q: Do Shiba Inus get along with other dogs?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can be selective with other dogs due to their protective nature. Early socialisation in puppy classes and controlled on-lead introductions with other dogs help build positive associations.

faqs.q: Do Shiba Inus bark a lot?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus tend to be vocal — they may bark at strangers, sounds, or when under-stimulated. Adequate daily exercise and mental enrichment (training sessions, puzzle feeders) significantly reduce nuisance barking. Teaching a "quiet" cue early is worthwhile.

faqs.q: Are Shiba Inus good apartment dogs?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus adapt reasonably well to apartment living, particularly if they receive consistent daily walks and indoor enrichment. Their compact nature makes them less disruptive in confined spaces than high-energy large breeds.

faqs.q: How much exercise does a Shiba Inu need per day?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus need approximately 45–60 minutes of exercise daily. A structured morning walk and an evening sniff walk usually cover their needs. Mental exercise (training sessions, puzzle feeders) counts toward overall stimulation needs and can reduce restless behaviour.

faqs.q: Are Shiba Inus good running partners?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can join you for moderate runs once fully grown. They're better suited to steady 3–5 mile runs than extended distance. Watch for signs of fatigue and always run in cooler hours during summer.

faqs.q: What happens if a Shiba Inu doesn't get enough exercise?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus are less demanding than high-energy breeds, but chronic under-exercise still leads to weight gain and low-level restlessness. Even lower-energy breeds benefit from a consistent daily walk for both physical health and mental stimulation.

faqs.q: Can a Shiba Inu be off-lead?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can be off-lead in secure areas once recall is reliable. Reliable recall typically takes 3–4 months of consistent training with progressive distance and distractions. Never trust off-lead recall in an unfenced area until it's been tested in controlled conditions first.

faqs.q: How much should I feed my Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: A Shiba Inu needs approximately ½–1½ cups of dry food per day for an adult, split across two meals. Always follow the feeding guide on your specific formula — calorie density varies significantly between brands. Adjust portions based on body condition: you should be able to feel (but not easily see) the ribs.

faqs.q: How many times a day should I feed a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Adult Shiba Inus should eat twice daily. Puppies (under 6 months) need 3–4 smaller meals per day to support growth and prevent hypoglycaemia, particularly in small breeds.

faqs.q: What is the best food for a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Look for a formula carrying an AAFCO adequacy statement for the correct life stage. A named protein source (chicken, turkey, beef, salmon) should appear first in the ingredient list. Medium-energy Shiba Inus do well on standard adult maintenance formulas with named protein as the first ingredient.

faqs.q: When should I switch my Shiba Inu from puppy to adult food?
faqs.a: Small breeds typically transition to adult food around 12 months. Moving too late keeps them on higher-calorie puppy formulas that can cause weight gain in lower-activity adults.

faqs.q: Is a Shiba Inu a good dog for first-time owners?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can be challenging for first-time owners due to their independent temperament. Prior dog experience or professional training classes from the start significantly improves outcomes. Research the breed thoroughly before committing.

faqs.q: Are Shiba Inus good family dogs?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus can be good family dogs when properly socialised. Their suitability depends more on individual temperament and upbringing than breed alone.

faqs.q: Do Shiba Inus do well when left alone?
faqs.a: Shiba Inus form strong bonds with their owners and do not do well with extended isolation. Aim for no more than 4–6 hours alone at a time. If your schedule requires longer absences, consider a dog walker, doggy daycare, or a companion dog.

faqs.q: How much time do you need for a Shiba Inu?
faqs.a: Plan for 1.5–2 hours per day dedicated to your Shiba Inu — covering exercise, training, feeding and general interaction.  The commitment is consistent year-round, not just when convenient.
